messages.content:
Positive real numbers \( x, y, \) and \( z \) satisfy the following equations:

\[
xyz = 3,
\]
\[
(x-y)(y-z)(z-x) = 4,
\]
\[
(x+y)(y+z)(z+x) = 40.
\]

Compute the minimum possible value for \( x \).

Give the minimum value of x as an exact expression using only integers, rational numbers, and radicals (no trigonometric or inverse trigonometric functions, and no approximations).

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
P=x+y+z,\qquad Q=xy+yz+zx.
\]

We are given \(xyz=3\). Also,

\[
(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)=PQ-xyz=PQ-3=40,
\]

so

\[
PQ=43. \tag{1}
\]

For the cubic with roots \(x,y,z\), the squared Vandermonde is

\[
(x-y)^2(y-z)^2(z-x)^2
=
P^2Q^2-4Q^3-12P^3-243+54PQ.
\]

Since \((x-y)(y-z)(z-x)=4\), the left side is \(16\). Using \(PQ=43\),

\[
1849-4Q^3-12P^3-243+2322=16,
\]

so

\[
Q^3+3P^3=978. \tag{2}
\]

Let \(S=P^3\). From (1), \(Q=43/P\), so \(Q^3=43^3/S=79507/S\). Equation (2) becomes

\[
\frac{79507}{S}+3S=978,
\]

or

\[
3S^2-978S+79507=0.
\]

Thus

\[
S=\frac{978\pm 20\sqrt6}{6}=163\pm \frac{10\sqrt6}{3}.
\]

So there are two possible symmetric-sum cases. In either case, the possible values of \(x\) are positive roots of

\[
t^3-Pt^2+Qt-3=0.
\]

Now let \(u=t^3\). If \(t_1,t_2,t_3\) are the three roots, then the cubic whose roots are \(u_i=t_i^3\) is

\[
u^3-\left(\sum t_i^3\right)u^2+\left(\sum (t_i t_j)^3\right)u-(t_1t_2t_3)^3=0.
\]

We have

\[
\sum t_i^3=P^3-3PQ+9=S-120,
\]

and

\[
\sum (t_i t_j)^3=Q^3-9PQ+27=Q^3-360.
\]

Since \(Q^3=79507/S=978-3S\), this equals \(618-3S\). Also \((t_1t_2t_3)^3=27\). Therefore the roots \(u=x^3\) satisfy

\[
u^3-(S-120)u^2+(618-3S)u-27=0. \tag{3}
\]

Let \(\alpha=\sqrt6\).

---

### Case 1: \(S=163-\frac{10\alpha}{3}\)

Then (3) becomes

\[
u^3-\left(43-\frac{10\alpha}{3}\right)u^2+(129+10\alpha)u-27=0.
\]

This factors as

\[
\left(u-\frac{3-\alpha}{3}\right)
\left(u^2-(42-3\alpha)u+81+27\alpha\right)=0.
\]

The quadratic has positive roots. Their product is \(81+27\alpha\), and their sum is \(42-3\alpha\). Since the product is greater than the sum, both roots are \(>1\). But

\[
0<\frac{3-\alpha}{3}<1.
\]

Thus the smallest possible \(u\) in this case is

\[
u_0=\frac{3-\sqrt6}{3}.
\]

---

### Case 2: \(S=163+\frac{10\alpha}{3}\)

Then (3) becomes

\[
u^3-\left(43+\frac{10\alpha}{3}\right)u^2+(129-10\alpha)u-27=0,
\]

which factors as

\[
\left(u-\frac{3+\alpha}{3}\right)
\left(u^2-(42+3\alpha)u+81-27\alpha\right)=0.
\]

The linear root \(\frac{3+\alpha}{3}>1\). For the quadratic

\[
q(u)=u^2-(42+3\alpha)u+81-27\alpha,
\]

we have

\[
q(0)=81-27\alpha>0,
\]

\[
q\!\left(\frac{3-\alpha}{3}\right)=\frac{140-50\alpha}{3}>0,
\]

and

\[
q(1)=40-30\alpha<0.
\]

Hence the smaller positive root of this quadratic lies between \(\frac{3-\alpha}{3}\) and \(1\), and the larger root is \(>1\). Therefore every root in this case is strictly larger than

\[
\frac{3-\sqrt6}{3}.
\]

---

Since \(u=x^3\) is increasing for positive \(x\), the minimum possible value of \(x\) is

\[
\sqrt[3]{\frac{3-\sqrt6}{3}}.
\]

This value is attainable by taking the three positive roots in increasing order, which makes \((x-y)(y-z)(z-x)>0\), hence equal to \(4\).

\[
\boxed{\sqrt[3]{\frac{3-\sqrt6}{3}}}
\]
